title: Is It a Well-Formed Number
statement:
A form field accepts numbers written in decimal or scientific notation. Decide whether the string s is a well-formed number under these rules:

  • It starts with a mantissa: an optional sign (+ or -), then digits with at most one dot . somewhere among them. The mantissa needs at least one digit, on either side of the dot. So "12", "12.", ".5" and "3.25" are fine, but "." is not.
  • It may then have an exponent: the letter e or E, then an optional sign, then at least one digit. No dot is allowed in the exponent.
  • Nothing else may appear: no spaces, no other letters, no extra signs.

Return true if s follows the rules, otherwise false.

examples.why: Sign, mantissa 3.75, then an exponent with its own sign and a digit.
The mantissa "+." has no digit at all, so the exponent has nothing to attach to.
The exponent must be a whole number. A dot after the e is not allowed.

constraints: s contains only English letters, digits, '+', '-' and '.'
hints: Read the rules as a grammar: [sign] mantissa [ (e|E) [sign] digits ]. Track what you have seen so far as you scan left to right.
Three flags are enough: seen a digit, seen a dot, seen an exponent. Each character is only legal in some combinations of those flags.

A sign is legal only at index 0 or right after e/E. A dot is legal only before any dot and before any e. An e is legal only once and only after a digit, and it resets the 'seen a digit' flag so the exponent must bring its own. At the end, you need 'seen a digit' to be true.

explain.intuition:
Trying to list every bad case leads to a pile of special cases. Instead, scan once and keep a small state that says what is allowed next. Three flags are enough: digit (a digit seen in the current part), dot (a dot seen), exp (an e seen).

Each character is then a single check. A digit is always fine and sets digit. A sign must be the first character, or come right after an e. A dot is fine only if there was no dot and no e before it. An e is fine only if there was no e before and the mantissa had a digit. It then clears digit, because the exponent must have its own digits. Anything else is invalid. At the end, the string is valid exactly when digit is set. This is a finite state machine written with flags, the same idea as a hand-written tokenizer or a form validator that runs on every keystroke.
steps: For each index i and character c: if c is a digit, set digit = true.
If c is + or -: valid only when i == 0 or s[i − 1] is e/E.
If c is .: valid only when !dot && !exp; set dot = true.
If c is e/E: valid only when !exp && digit; set exp = true and digit = false. Any other character returns false.
pitfalls: Forgetting to clear digit at the e. Then "1e" passes, because the mantissa's digit is still counted.
Rejecting "5." or ".5". One digit on either side of the dot is enough; only a bare "." fails.
Using the language's own number parser. Number("") is 0, Number("0x1F") is 31 and Number(" 7 ") is 7 in JavaScript, and Python's float accepts "inf" and "1_0". None of those follow these rules.

solutions.title: One pass with three flags
solutions.idea: Scan left to right remembering whether a digit, a dot and an e have appeared. Each character is legal only in some states.

solutions.title: Regular expression
solutions.idea: The grammar is regular, so one anchored pattern states it directly. Short, but be ready to explain every part of it.

followups: Also allow leading and trailing spaces, and hexadecimal integers like 0x1F. How does the state machine grow?
Rewrite the flag solution as an explicit table of states and transitions. Which version would you rather maintain?
